forms.name: Gond
forms.what: Animals and trees in thin black outline, filled with bold flat colour in bands, each band carrying fine repeated marks of one colour: dots, dashes, parallel lines or fish-scale arcs. A plain light ground, a bold crest and a decorated eye. It is a living tradition with working artists; the demo here is a code study of its visual rules, not the craft itself, and a film should credit the tradition and, where it can, commission or license work from the artists.
forms.origin: The Gond, or Gondi, people are an ethnolinguistic group spread across central and eastern India, including Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Chhattisgarh. The artist Jangarh Singh Shyam, born into a Pardhan Gond family in Patangarh, Mandla district, Madhya Pradesh, is credited with starting the school called Jangarh Kalam; he used lines of coloured dots, inspired by Gond tattoos, with bands of dots, dense cross-hatching and comb-lines, and painted animals such as tigers and deer.
rules: Thin black outlines round animals, birds and trees
Saturated flat colour: deep red, saffron, cobalt, leaf green and black
Each body is filled in bands; each band is a solid base colour with marks of ONE contrasting colour, never a rainbow inside a stripe
Mark types alternate band by band: rows of dots, short dashes, fine parallel lines, fish-scale arcs
Bold, decorated details: a crest, an eye with rings and dots, branches that curl in toward the animal
forms.timing: Parts draw on one after another over about 3 seconds, outline first, then the bands fill. The picture steps about 8 times a second.
build: Draw each part with `folkShape()` and a black fill under the bands
Bands: rotate to the shape's long axis, fill a 14 px strip with the base colour, then draw one mark type in the paired colour (`gondBands()` and the `GOND` colour pairs in `looks-folk.js`)
Trunks and branches: a tapering band along a spline (`ribbon()`), ending in a curl
Eye: a pale ring, a red ring, a dark pupil and a ring of small dots
Keep the ground plain; add only a dotted border
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: Drums and a stringed drone, a rhythmic tapping as each band fills. Practice note.
pitfalls: Pastel stripes or a rainbow inside each band: the colours are saturated and each band has one mark colour
Gradients and shading
Presenting a machine-made picture as authentic Gond art
forms.thin: Wikipedia has no standalone Gond painting article, so the sources are the Gond people article and the article on Jangarh Singh Shyam, the artist most closely tied to the modern style. Confirm the wider tradition against a museum source before making claims in a film.

forms.name: Indian miniature (Mughal and Rajput)
forms.what: A small, richly detailed court painting in jewel tones: a flat, stacked space with no deep perspective, a gold border with a floral margin, fine ornament on every surface, and figures in profile. It is a living tradition with working artists; the demo here is a code study of its visual rules, not the craft itself, and a film should credit the tradition and, where it can, commission or license work from the artists.
forms.origin: Mughal painting is a style of miniature painting, used for book illustrations and album pages, that developed at the Mughal court between the 16th and 19th centuries; its portraits are normally in profile. Rajput painting is the painting of the regional Hindu courts during the Mughal era, from about the end of the 16th to the middle of the 19th century, and its conservative idioms keep bright colour, flatness and abstract form.
rules: Flat, stacked space: sky, palace, terrace and garden as bands, no deep perspective
Jewel tones: ruby, emerald, lapis, saffron and gold
A gold border with a floral margin, drawn as part of the painting
Figures in profile, small and seated, with turbans and robes
Fine ornament: domes, arches, flower beds, water channels
forms.timing: The border, the sky and the palace draw in over about 2 seconds, then the garden, water and figures. Birds drift and the fountain rises. The picture steps about 8 times a second.
build: Paint bands from back to front, each a flat fill with a thin dark line
Border: a ruby frame between gold lines with a row of small flowers (`rosette()`)
Domes: half-ellipses with ribs, a finial and a small disc
Figures: a robe polygon, a profile head with a nose notch, a turban ellipse and one arm to a cup
Animate only small things: birds, the fountain, the cloud ribbons
forms.assets: All in code. For real pages use public-domain scans from museum collections and say so in REPORT.md.
forms.sound: Sitar or santoor, a quiet fountain, birdsong. Practice note.
pitfalls: Deep one-point perspective and cast shadows
Photorealistic faces
Presenting a machine-made picture as authentic Mughal or Rajput work

forms.name: Engraving and banknote hatching
forms.what: Fine lines cut like a burin: hatching that follows the form and swells in the shadow, cross-hatching where it is darkest, a vignette of waves, and a woven guilloche frame, in one or two inks on cream paper.
forms.origin: Engraving is the practice of incising a design on a hard surface with a burin; the grooves can make an intaglio plate for printing. In traditional engraving, which is a purely linear medium, half-tones are made by many thin parallel lines, hatching, and two crossing sets of them are cross-hatching. Guilloché is a precise, repetitive pattern engraved by engine turning, and modern banknotes are almost always engraved.
rules: Tone from line only: thin lines in the light, thick lines in the shadow
Lines follow the form: curved round a sphere, not straight across it
Cross-hatching only in the deepest shade
A guilloche frame of interwoven waves and rosettes
One or two inks: a dark brown-black and a burgundy on cream paper
forms.timing: Lines are cut one after another from top to bottom over about 3 seconds, then the cross-hatching and frame. Full frame rate: an engraved line should not step.
build: Sphere: sample points with latitude, longitude and a tilt, and a brightness from a light direction (`spherePoint()` in `looks-folk.js`)
Stroke each short segment with a width of about `0.35 + 3.3 * (1 - brightness) ** 1.7`
Cross-hatch: a second family of lines drawn only where brightness is under 0.4
Guilloche: six sine waves in different phases across each side, and a rose curve at each corner
Background vignette: horizontal wavy lines whose width grows toward the edge, clipped to an ellipse
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: A fine scratch under the line work, a quiet low tone. Practice note.
pitfalls: Lines of one width: the swelling is the engraving
Smooth gradients
Straight hatching that ignores the form

forms.name: Silkscreen poster
forms.what: A poster printed in a few flat inks that overprint, each a little out of register, with coarse halftone dots for tone: flat shapes, big blocks, and colours that mix where they overlap.
forms.origin: Screen printing, also silkscreening or serigraphy, transfers ink through a mesh onto a surface except where a stencil blocks it; traditionally the mesh was silk. It is widely used for posters and other graphics.
rules: Two to four flat inks, never more
Inks overprint with multiply, so overlaps make new colours
Each ink is a little off register, differently on each drawing
Halftone dots at an angle for gradients and glows
Bold flat shapes and block bars where type would go
Paper grain showing through
forms.timing: Each ink prints in turn, sliding into register over about 0.7 seconds, one every second. The picture steps about 8 times a second and each step re-seeds the misregistration.
build: One draw function per ink, drawn with `globalCompositeOperation = 'multiply'` (`inkLayer()` in `looks-folk.js`)
Offset each layer by a few pixels plus a seeded jitter keyed to `frameOf(t, 8)`
Halftone: a rotated grid of dots whose radius is `pitch * 0.72 * sqrt(value)` (`halftone()`)
Slide each layer in from off-register and settle it at its offset
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: A press clunk and a squeegee sweep as each ink lands, an upbeat drum loop. Practice note.
pitfalls: Perfect register and soft gradients: that reads as digital
Too many colours
Transparency that does not multiply

forms.name: Art deco
forms.what: Gold lines, sunbursts and stepped, symmetric geometry on a deep ground: fans and arcs, a tower in steps, zigzag borders and small stars, in gold on navy and burgundy.
forms.origin: Art Deco first appeared in Paris in the 1910s, just before the First World War, and flourished internationally in the 1920s and early 1930s; the name came into use after the 1925 Paris exhibition of decorative and industrial arts. It has its origin in the bold geometric forms of the Vienna Secession and Cubism, and in New York the Empire State and Chrysler Buildings are monuments to the style.
rules: Strict symmetry about a vertical axis
Gold or light-gold lines on a deep ground: black, navy, burgundy or emerald
Sunburst rays, fans and concentric arcs
Stepped shapes: towers and frames in steps
Zigzag borders, chevrons and small star sparkles
forms.timing: Rays and arcs grow out from the centre over about 3 seconds, then the tower rises in steps. Smooth, full frame rate, with a slow twinkle.
build: Sunburst: wedges that alternate fill and ground, each edge a gold line drawn to a growing radius
Arcs: `ctx.arc` from pi to a growing angle at several radii
Tower: nested rectangles of falling width, each rising in turn
Mirror the side decoration with `ctx.scale(-1, 1)` so it is exactly symmetric
Sparkles: eight-point stars whose size follows a sine of time
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: Brass and muted trumpet, a swing bed. Practice note.
pitfalls: Asymmetry
Soft gradients and rounded shapes
Using teal or mint: this skill leaves them out

forms.name: Stained glass
forms.what: Coloured panes held by thick dark lead lines in an arched window: a rose at the top, a diamond lattice below, and light glowing through each pane.
forms.origin: Stained glass is glass coloured by adding metallic salts during its manufacture, arranged into windows of small pieces held together, traditionally, by strips of lead called cames. In Western Europe, together with illuminated manuscripts, such windows are a major form of medieval visual art that has survived.
rules: Thick, dark, even lead lines round every pane
Saturated, jewel-coloured panes: ruby, cobalt, emerald, amber, violet
Each pane glows brighter at its centre, as light passes through
A pointed or round arch, with a rose and a lattice
A dark stone wall round it, so the glass is the light source
forms.timing: The panes light up from the centre outward over about 2 seconds, then a soft beam of sun crosses the glass slowly. Smooth, full frame rate.
build: Build each pane as a polygon; fill dark, then fill with its colour as it is lit, plus a radial glow with `lighter`
Rose: annular sectors in three rings (`ring()` in the demo); lattice: a grid of diamonds clipped to the arch
Stroke every pane with a 6 px dark line, `lineJoin = 'round'`
The beam: a linear gradient band drawn with `lighter`, its position a function of time
Wall: dark base colour and a block pattern
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: A choir pad, a long reverb, footsteps in a stone room. Practice note.
pitfalls: Thin lead lines: they are part of the picture
Flat panes with no glow
Washed-out pastel colours: keep them saturated

forms.name: Retro anime (80s and 90s)
forms.what: A hand-painted television look: hard two-tone shading, banded sunset skies, a striped sun, a lit skyline, a figure from behind with hair and scarf in the wind, a little film grain and a soft glow.
forms.origin: Anime is animation originating from Japan; a characteristic art style emerged in the 1960s and spread in the following decades. Traditional animation paints the characters on transparent cels laid over a static painted background, a process generally credited to Earl Hurd, who patented it in 1914.
rules: Hard-edged two-tone shading: one base colour and one shadow colour, no soft gradients on the characters
Banded, graded skies in stepped colour: violet to magenta to orange to cream
A big sun with horizontal slits, a lit skyline, a rim of warm light on the edges
Characters seen from behind or in profile, hair and scarf moving in the wind
Film grain, and a soft bloom around bright areas
forms.timing: Drawn on threes: about 8 changes a second inside a 24 frames-a-second film. The sun rises slowly, windows twinkle and hair streams.
build: Quantise time with `held(t, 8)` and key every flicker to `frameOf(t, 8)`
Sky: eight flat bands from `fillRect`; the sun is a clipped disc with a hard shadow tone and slits cut across it
Shade a character with a base polygon and a second polygon of the shadow colour on one side
Bloom: a radial gradient drawn with `lighter` over the picture; grain: a speckle with a seed from `frameOf(t, 8) % 6`
forms.assets: All in code. For real character art, paint on layers and keep the shadow tone as its own layer.
forms.sound: A synth pad and a drum machine, city ambience, wind on the rooftop. Practice note.
pitfalls: Smooth gradients on the figures: the shading is hard-edged
Smooth 24 frames-a-second motion on every layer, which loses the television feel
Copying a recognisable character
forms.route: HyperFrames (canvas), or Blender with a toon material for 3D

forms.name: Manga (black and white with screentone)
forms.what: Black and white only: inked panels with thick borders, screentone dots for grey, speed lines and bursts, and one dramatic moment drawn large.
forms.origin: Manga are comics or graphic novels originating from Japan; most conform to a style developed in Japan in the late 19th century, with a long history in earlier Japanese art.
rules: Pure black and pure white: no greys and no colour
Panels with thick black borders and uneven sizes: one big panel for the moment, smaller ones around it
Tone: halftone dots of one size per area, at a slant, for shadow and mood
Speed lines that converge on the point of impact; a burst shape for the hit
Bold line weights and spiky hair; faces in extreme close-up for emotion
forms.timing: Panels slam in one after another, 0.1 to 2.2 seconds, and the speed lines re-roll about 8 times a second. Stepped, not smooth.
build: Each panel: a clipped rectangle that scales from 1.12 to 1 with `easeOut` as it appears
Speed lines: thin black wedges between two radii with a seeded length per line, re-seeded on each step (`speedLines()` in `looks-toon.js`)
Screentone: a rotated dot grid whose radius follows a value function (`halftone()` in `looks-folk.js`)
Draw figures from local coordinates and mirror them for the second fighter
Use only `#000` and `#fff`: no antialiased greys except at edges
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: Sharp impact hits, a sword-ring or a drum, silence between panels. Practice note.
pitfalls: Any grey or colour
Panels that are all the same size
Speed lines that do not converge on the action

forms.name: Chibi
forms.what: A character two or three heads tall: a huge head, a tiny body, big shiny eyes, rosy cheeks and a bounce with a real squash and stretch.
forms.origin: Chibi, also known as super deformation (SD), is an art style originating in Japan and common in anime and manga, where characters are drawn small and chubby with stubby limbs, oversized eyes and heads, tiny noses and bodies, and minimal detail. The word comes from chibi kyara, "tiny character".
rules: The head is as wide as the body is tall: two to three heads high
Big eyes with a gradient iris and two highlights; tiny nose and mouth
Stubby limbs and minimal detail on the body
Soft rounded outlines in a darker shade of the fill, not black
Bounce with squash on landing and stretch in the air
forms.timing: A bounce about once a second on twos (12 changes a second), with a blink every 2 to 3 seconds.
build: Pose the whole character in local coordinates and apply `ctx.scale(1 + s, 1 - s)` about the feet, where `s` follows the landing and the air time
Eyes: a white ellipse, a radial-gradient iris, a dark pupil, two white highlight discs and a heavy upper lash arc
Twin tails swing by an angle that follows the bounce
Floating star sparkles drift by stepped time
forms.assets: All in code. Original characters only: do not trace an existing one.
forms.sound: A bright, bouncy pop track, a spring boing on each landing. Practice note.
pitfalls: A body longer than the head
Squash with no matching stretch
Copying a recognisable character

forms.name: Ukiyo-e woodblock
forms.what: A Japanese woodblock print: flat areas of colour, fine ink outlines, a great curling wave of deep blue with claw-like fingers of foam, a pale banded sky, a small distant mountain and a red seal.
forms.origin: Ukiyo-e is a genre of Japanese art that flourished from the 17th through 19th centuries, with woodblock prints and paintings; the term means "pictures of the floating world". By the 1740s artists were using several blocks to print areas of colour, and Hokusai's The Great Wave off Kanagawa is one of the best-known works of Japanese art.
rules: Flat colour areas, no gradients except a soft band at the top of the sky
Fine ink outlines round every shape
A deep Prussian-style blue for water, with darker contour lines that follow the wave
Foam as claw-like white fingers curling from the crest, with a few spray dots
A small mountain far away, a red seal, a thin border, paper grain
forms.timing: The wave rises and the foam fingers grow over about 2 seconds; the sea and boats bob gently. The picture steps about 8 times a second.
build: Wave: a closed spline through hand-placed points (`closed()`), filled and outlined
Contour lines: scale the same outline about its centre several times and clip them to the wave
Foam fingers: tapering bands along short curves (`ribbon()`), one per crest point, growing in turn
Sea: a polyline whose height follows a sine of stepped time
Add paper grain with `speckle()`
forms.assets: All in code. Public-domain scans of historic prints are a better source for real prints; check the museum's terms.
forms.sound: A shamisen and a taiko, the sound of surf. Practice note.
pitfalls: Smooth shading and gradients on the water
Thick or uneven outlines: the lines are fine
Copying an existing print: the demo is an original study
forms.thin: Wikipedia's ukiyo-e article does not describe Prussian blue, wave contour lines or claw-like foam; those rules are a practice summary from looking at the genre, not sourced facts.

forms.name: Modern TV cartoon
forms.what: Thick, even outlines and flat, bright colour on simple geometric characters: squares, circles and triangles with big eyes, bouncing on twos against a plain, flat background.
forms.origin: In the animation sense a cartoon is a motion picture that relies on a sequence of illustrations. Limited animation reuses frames of character animation to save time and money, and in the late 1990s web animators using cutout and limited animation produced clean, vector-graphic pictures at small file sizes.
rules: One thick outline weight round everything, in a near-black
Flat, saturated colour with no shading or only one flat shadow
Characters built from simple shapes: squares, circles, triangles
Big round eyes with a small pupil; a simple wide mouth
Plain, flat backgrounds: a hill, a cloud, a sun, a tree
forms.timing: Drawn on twos, 12 changes a second, with holds, bounces and a blink every couple of seconds.
build: Draw each shape with a fill and an 8 px outline of the same dark colour (`ell()` and `polyFill()` in `looks-toon.js`)
Bounce: a parabola from the cycle phase, with a squash of a few percent at landing
Blink: replace the eye with a line for 0.15 seconds
Limbs are single thick strokes with a circle at the end
Keep the palette to six or seven colours
forms.assets: All in code. Original characters only.
forms.sound: A quick jazz or brass bed with a boing on each bounce. Practice note.
pitfalls: Gradients, textures and thin outlines
Realistic proportions
Copying a recognisable show's characters

forms.name: Gothic cartoon
forms.what: Spindly, hollow-eyed figures and crooked houses with lit windows under a pale moon, curly trees and bats, in purple and black: a cartoon that is spooky and funny at once.
forms.origin: Gothic fiction is a literary aesthetic of fear and haunting; the name comes from the Renaissance use of "gothic" for the medieval and barbaric, and the first work labelled Gothic was Horace Walpole's 1764 novel The Castle of Otranto.
rules: Tall, thin figures with long limbs, big heads, hollow eyes and spiky hair
Crooked houses and trees: nothing stands straight; roofs are tall and pointed
A palette of purple and near-black with a pale moon and a few lit windows
Curly, spiral branches and moon marks
Bats, stars and a low fog, with everything swaying a little
forms.timing: Everything sways on twos, about 8 changes a second: houses lean back and forth, trees swing, figures step and bats flap.
build: Lean every house with `ctx.transform(1, 0, lean, 1, 0, 0)` where `lean` is a small sine of stepped time plus a fixed tilt
Trees: a curved trunk with spiral ends from `curlPts()`
Figures: thin rectangles and strokes in local coordinates, scaled for depth
A fog gradient across the ground and a few flickering windows
forms.assets: All in code. Original characters only.
forms.sound: A creaking harpsichord or a music box, a distant wolf, wind. Practice note.
pitfalls: Straight lines and symmetric buildings
Bright, cheerful colour
Copying a recognisable character or a studio's house style
forms.thin: No source on the page describes a gothic cartoon look; the rules are a practice summary. The origin line is only the root of the word.

forms.name: Pop-up book
forms.what: An open book seen at an angle: the pages swing open and layered card pieces stand up off them, each with a fold shadow, a visible card edge and a shadow on the page.
forms.origin: A pop-up book is any book with three-dimensional pages, often with elements that pop up as a page is turned; designing them is sometimes called paper engineering. The first known movable in a book was made by the Benedictine monk Matthew Paris, whose Chronica Majora, covering a period beginning in 1240, had volvelles attached to some pages.
rules: A book at an angle with a spine shadow and a cover edge
Card pieces that stand up from the pages in layers, near and far
A thin offset edge and a fold shadow where each piece meets the page
A shadow on the page under each piece
Bright, flat, paper-craft colours
forms.timing: The right page swings open over about 1.2 seconds, then each piece pops up in turn with a slight overshoot. Smooth motion.
build: Map page space to the screen with a perspective-like function: width narrows toward the back, and `cos(pi (1 - open))` swings the right page
Each piece: a draw function in its own local coordinates, scaled vertically by an overshooting `k`
Draw the piece twice: a dark copy offset sideways as the card edge, then the front
A small ellipse shadow and a gradient fold shadow at the base
Sort pieces back to front
forms.assets: All in code. For a real pop-up, build it in Blender with folded geometry.
forms.sound: A page turn, a paper pop and a music-box bed. Practice note.
pitfalls: Pieces that float: each needs a base on the page and a shadow
No overshoot on the pop
A flat book with no angle
forms.route: HyperFrames (canvas), Blender for real folded paper

forms.name: Papercut and sanjhi (lace-cut paper)
forms.what: One colour of cut paper on a plain ground: a scalloped medallion and corner pieces full of symmetrical cut-outs, with a soft shadow that shows the paper is a layer above the page. It is a living tradition with working artists; the demo here is a code study of its visual rules, not the craft itself.
forms.origin: Papercutting is the art of making designs cut from a single sheet of paper, which has developed in many cultures; the oldest surviving paper cutout, a symmetrical circle from the 6th century, was found in Xinjiang, China. Japanese paper cutting is called kirigami.
rules: One paper colour only: red on cream, or white on a dark ground
Symmetry: radial for a medallion, mirrored for corners
Cut-outs in rings: leaves, drops, round holes, fine dots
A scalloped or pointed edge and thin bridges between the holes
A slight drop shadow and a trace of sway
forms.timing: The rings open one after another over about 3 seconds, and the paper trembles a fraction of a degree. The picture steps about 8 times a second.
build: One `Path2D`: the outline plus every hole as a subpath, filled with the even-odd rule (`holesPath()` in `looks-toon.js`)
Rings of holes by `laceRing()`: leaf, drop and dot shapes at equal angles, scaled up from nothing to open them
Shadow: `shadowBlur`, `shadowOffsetX` and `shadowOffsetY` on the fill
Mirror a corner piece four ways with `ctx.scale(+-1, +-1)`
forms.assets: All in code. A scanned sheet of cream paper helps if the user has one.
forms.sound: A scissors snip as each ring opens, a soft drone. Practice note.
pitfalls: Two or more colours: that is collage, not a single sheet
Holes with no bridges, which would fall apart
Presenting a machine-made picture as authentic sanjhi work
forms.thin: The sources do not cover sanjhi, the Indian stencil papercutting tradition: it is named here only as an alias. Add a primary or museum source for it before a film makes claims about it.

forms.name: Brick toy
forms.what: Everything built from studded plastic bricks on a green baseplate: visible studs, a glossy edge, flat bright colours, and bricks that drop in one at a time on twos.
forms.origin: Brick toys are a kind of construction set: a standardised assortment of pieces for building models, most often marketed as toys.
rules: Every object is made of rectangular bricks on a stud grid
A baseplate with a stud on every cell
Flat, bright primary colours with a lighter top and darker sides
A bright edge and a glossy highlight on the studs
Models built layer by layer, brick by brick
forms.timing: Bricks drop in one at a time over about 4 seconds, each falling about six layers and settling. Drawn on twos, 12 changes a second.
build: An isometric projection: `sx = cx + (x - y) * cw`, `sy = cy + (x + y) * ch - z * bh` (`iso()` in `looks-toon.js`)
Each brick: a top and two sides in three shades of one colour, then a stud on each cell (`brick()`, `stud()`)
Sort bricks by `x + y` then by height so that nearer bricks cover farther ones
Drop each brick with `easeOut` from above and fade it in
forms.assets: All in code. No logos, no brand names, no printed lettering on the studs.
forms.sound: Click and clack of plastic, a cheerful ukulele bed. Practice note.
pitfalls: Smooth sloped surfaces: only bricks and plates
No studs
Any brand name or logo
forms.thin: The source describes construction sets in general. Brand names appear only in the router keywords, so that the router understands a request; they are never used in a name, a rule or a picture.

forms.name: String puppet and kathputli
forms.what: Marionettes in bright Rajasthani dress: big painted wooden heads, turbans and ghagras, strings to a control bar at the top, jerky dangling motion, in a small theatre with red curtains and a gold valance. It is a living tradition with working artists; the demo here is a code study of its visual rules, not the craft itself.
forms.origin: Kathputli is a string puppet theatre native to Rajasthan, India, and the most popular form of Indian puppetry; the name means a wooden doll, and the puppets are made of wood, cotton cloth and metal wire. A marionette, or string puppet, is controlled from above using wires or strings and a controller; puppetry is recorded in Ancient Greece in the 5th century BC.
rules: A large, painted head with big eyes, strong brows and a moustache for the king, a veil and nose ring for the dancer
Bright costume: red turban and yellow tunic, a pink and orange gathered skirt with gold trim
Strings run straight from a bar at the top to the head, hands and feet
Jerky, swinging limbs, as if on strings, with the whole puppet swaying
A small stage with red curtains, a gold valance and a plank floor
forms.timing: The limbs swing on twos, about 8 changes a second, each with its own phase, and the bar tilts slowly.
build: Compute each hand and foot from a swinging angle (`puppet()` in `looks-toon.js`), then draw the strings from the bar anchors to those points first
Body parts as polygons and strokes in local coordinates, with an outline
Stage: stripes, an arch, two curtain drapes with gold fringe and a scalloped valance
Use stepped time `held(t, 8)` so the motion is jerky
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: Dholak and harmonium, folk song, the wooden clack of puppets. Practice note.
pitfalls: Smooth, floaty limbs: marionettes swing and stop
Strings that do not reach the limbs
Presenting a machine-made picture as an authentic kathputli show
forms.thin: Wikipedia describes the Kathputli as worked by a single string over the puppeteer; the demo uses a Western-style control bar, with strings to the head, hands and feet, so that the strings are easy to read. Check a real rig before a film shows one.

forms.name: Stylised 3D cartoon
forms.what: A soft, rounded 3D cartoon character or prop with a big readable face: smooth forms, a soft key light, a cool rim light and warm light that seems to pass through the skin. The demo is drawn in 2D, so it renders with no WebGL; the Three.js recipe below is how to build the real thing.
forms.origin: Three-point lighting is a standard method in film, photography and 3D graphics: the key light is the principal illuminator, usually 30 to 45 degrees to one side of the camera and elevated about as much. Subsurface scattering is light travelling into a translucent surface and out again at another point; without it a material can look like plastic or metal.
rules: Smooth, rounded forms with no hard edges: spheres, capsules and soft boxes
A big, readable face: large eyes with a gradient and two highlights, clear brows, a wide mouth
A soft key light from the upper left, a cool rim light on the far edge, and a soft specular highlight
A warm glow at the shadow edge, as light bleeds through the skin
A shallow-depth background of blurred lights and a soft contact shadow
forms.timing: Smooth, full frame rate: a slow breath, a bounce, a blink every three seconds and a wave. The squash and stretch are small and soft.
build: Three.js: `MeshPhysicalMaterial` with `sheen`, a low `clearcoat`, and `transmission` or a warm emissive rim for the subsurface look
Lights: a `DirectionalLight` key at about 40 degrees, a cool back `DirectionalLight` for the rim, a `HemisphereLight` fill, and `ACESFilmicToneMapping`
Add `OutputPass` and a gentle `UnrealBloomPass`; soft `PCFSoftShadowMap` shadows
Add a shallow depth of field with `BokehPass`
In the 2D demo: `ball()` builds each form from an offset radial gradient, a warm inner gradient, a rim arc and a soft highlight
forms.assets: All in code here. For a real character, model it in Blender and export a glTF.
forms.sound: Soft foley, a light orchestral bed and a spring on each bounce. Practice note.
pitfalls: Hard black outlines: they turn it into toon 3D
Plastic highlights and no warm bleed at the shadow edge
A small face: the face must be readable at a glance
Copying a recognisable studio character
forms.thin: The two sources cover the lighting and shading ideas; the face and softness rules are a practice summary.

forms.name: Toon 3D (cel-shaded, comic-book)
forms.what: 3D forms cut into two or three flat shading bands, with a thick ink outline on every silhouette and a printed, painterly comic-book feel. The demo is drawn in 2D, so it renders with no WebGL; the Three.js recipe below is how to build the real thing.
forms.origin: Cel shading, or toon shading, is a type of non-photorealistic rendering that makes 3D graphics look flat and hand-drawn: conventional smooth lighting values are quantised to a few discrete shades, so that shadows and highlights appear as blocks of colour. Black ink outlines can be made by first rendering a slightly larger black copy of the object with its back faces drawn.
rules: Two or three flat bands of colour: a light, a base and a shadow, with hard edges
A thick ink outline round the silhouette
The shadow band tinted toward purple or blue, not just darker
Print texture: halftone dots, hatching lines and paper grain
A hard highlight spot and a hard-edged ground shadow
forms.timing: Smooth rotation and bounce at the full frame rate; or stepped on twos for a hand-drawn feel.
build: Three.js: `MeshToonMaterial` with a `gradientMap` of 3 texels (`DataTexture` with `NearestFilter`), so that lighting steps in three bands
Outlines: `OutlineEffect` from the examples, or draw a back-face copy scaled by 1.03 in black
Add a `HalftonePass`, or a halftone texture multiplied into the shadow band
Tint the shadow band in the gradient map toward purple
In the 2D demo: `turn()` rotates vertices, face normals pick one of three bands (`band3()`), and a thick ink stroke outlines each face
forms.assets: All in code here.
forms.sound: Brush-stroke whooshes and a drum loop. Practice note.
pitfalls: Smooth gradients inside the bands
Thin or uneven outlines
More than three bands: it starts to look like normal shading

forms.name: Point cloud and lidar scan
forms.what: An object or scene made of thousands of glowing points on black, in blue and gold, turning slowly, with points that fade and shrink as they recede. The demo is drawn in 2D, so it renders with no WebGL; the Three.js recipe below is how to build the real thing.
forms.origin: A point cloud is a discrete set of data points in space; each has X, Y and Z coordinates and may carry colour and other data. Point clouds are produced by 3D scanners or photogrammetry software. Lidar measures distance by timing the return of laser light, and is used to make high-resolution maps.
rules: Only points, no surfaces or lines
Glowing points on black, in two hues: blue for the ground, gold for the object
Depth: far points are smaller and dimmer
Scan structure: rings or lines of points, and a pulse of brighter points sweeping over them
A slow turn, a high camera, and a faint vignette
forms.timing: A slow turn at the full frame rate; the cloud builds up over about 1.6 seconds and the scan pulse crosses the ground every 3 to 4 seconds.
build: Three.js: `Points` with a `BufferGeometry`, `PointsMaterial` (`sizeAttenuation: true`, `vertexColors`, `AdditiveBlending`, `depthWrite: false`)
Size by depth in a custom shader: `gl_PointSize = base / -mvPosition.z`
Real data: load a PLY or PCD scan with the examples loaders
Scan pulse: a uniform radius that brightens the points near it
In the 2D demo: project each point with a turn, a tilt and a perspective factor, and draw it as a tiny square with `lighter` compositing (`plot()`)
forms.assets: All in code here. Real scans come from a lidar device or a photogrammetry run.
forms.sound: A low synth pulse and a soft ping as the scan passes. Practice note.
pitfalls: Joining the points with lines or surfaces
Opaque, same-sized points: no depth
Too few points: it reads as sparkle, not as an object

forms.name: Tilt-shift miniature diorama
forms.what: A tiny town seen from a high camera: saturated toy colours, little cars looping round the roads, and a blur that grows toward the top and bottom of the frame, so that it looks like a model. The demo is drawn in 2D, so it renders with no WebGL; the Three.js recipe below is how to build the real thing.
forms.origin: Tilt-shift photography uses camera movements that change the orientation or position of the lens relative to the sensor; the term is also used when a shallow depth of field is simulated in post-processing. A diorama is a replica of a scene, typically a three-dimensional model, miniature or full-size.
rules: A high camera looking down at an angle
A sharp band across the middle, with blur growing toward the top and bottom edges
Saturated, toy-like colours and simple blocky buildings
Tiny moving things: cars, boats or people
Soft, slightly raised contrast and a light vignette
forms.timing: Smooth: cars loop round the roads at different speeds, and the camera is still.
build: Three.js: an `OrthographicCamera` or a narrow-FOV `PerspectiveCamera` placed high, and `InstancedMesh` buildings
Tilt-shift: render to a target and blur it with a vertical mask, as in the `HorizontalTiltShiftShader` and `VerticalTiltShiftShader` examples, or use `BokehPass` with a focal band
Raise saturation and add a soft vignette with an `OutputPass` and a colour-grade pass
In the 2D demo: draw the town to an off-screen canvas, then draw it again through several clipped bands with increasing `blur()` (`diorama`)
forms.assets: All in code here.
forms.sound: A light ukulele bed and distant traffic noise. Practice note.
pitfalls: Blur across the whole frame, which reads as out of focus
Muted, realistic colours
A low camera: the miniature look needs a high angle

forms.name: Parallax 2.5D
forms.what: Four to six flat painted layers moving at different speeds as the camera pans: a sky, far mountains, hills, a row of trees, a field and grass in front, so that a flat scene feels deep. The demo is drawn in 2D, so it renders with no WebGL; the Three.js recipe below is how to build the real thing.
forms.origin: Parallax scrolling is a technique where background images move past the camera more slowly than foreground images, creating an illusion of depth in a 2D scene. It grew out of the multiplane camera used in traditional animation since the 1930s, which moved layers of artwork at different speeds and distances.
rules: Layers, each one flat: sky, far mountains, hills, trees, field, foreground
Each layer moves at its own speed: the nearer, the faster
Distant layers are hazier and lighter; near layers darker and more saturated
Layers repeat seamlessly as the camera pans
A fixed or very slow sky and sun
forms.timing: A steady pan to the right at about 90 px a second; speeds from 0.02 for the sun to 1.8 for the grass blades. Smooth, full frame rate.
build: Three.js: flat `PlaneGeometry` layers with textured `MeshBasicMaterial` at different `z` depths and a `PerspectiveCamera` moving along x, or the same layers with an orthographic camera scaling each layer's x motion
In the 2D demo: each layer is drawn in screen columns offset by `camera * speed`, wrapping with `Math.floor(offset / width)`, and ridges come from value noise of world x (`ridge()`)
Add atmospheric haze by mixing far layers toward the sky colour
Add a slight vertical bob to the camera
forms.assets: All in code here. For real layers, paint each on a transparent PNG.
forms.sound: Wind, birdsong, a gentle acoustic bed. Practice note.
pitfalls: All layers moving at the same speed
Visible seams where a layer repeats
Detail in the far layers that competes with the foreground

forms.name: Synthwave and outrun
forms.what: A neon night in magenta and cyan on deep purple: a striped sun sinking behind wireframe mountains, and a glowing grid floor that streams toward the horizon.
forms.origin: Synthwave, also called retrowave or futuresynth, is an electronic music microgenre based mainly on the music of action, science-fiction and horror film soundtracks of the 1970s and 1980s, and drawing on the decade's art and video games; it developed in the mid-to-late 2000s.
rules: A deep purple sky graded to hot pink at the horizon
A big sun with horizontal slits, in yellow to orange to magenta
A neon grid floor: lines that converge to a vanishing point and rows that bunch toward the horizon
Wireframe mountains outlined in cyan
Glow on every line, a bright horizon line, and a field of stars
forms.timing: The grid rows stream toward the camera continuously and the sun's slits creep down; smooth, full frame rate.
build: Floor rows: `y = horizon + (H - horizon) * ((k + phase) / n) ** 2.3`, with `phase` from time so the rows flow; columns are straight lines from the vanishing point
Glow: stroke twice with `shadowBlur`, a wide coloured pass and a thin white core (`neon()` in `looks-screen.js`)
Sun: a clipped disc with a vertical gradient and bars of the sky colour whose thickness grows toward the bottom
Use magenta and cyan only for lines: no mint
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: A pulsing analogue synth bass, gated reverb drums and an arpeggio. Practice note.
pitfalls: Mint or teal in place of cyan
A flat, unlit grid with no glow
Rows that do not bunch toward the horizon
forms.thin: The source describes the music genre; the neon grid and striped sun are the visual conventions that go with it, described here as practice.

forms.name: Cyberpunk night city
forms.what: A rainy night street in purple and amber: towers hung with flickering neon signs, a wet road that mirrors them, rain and ripples, and a lone figure under an umbrella.
forms.origin: Cyberpunk is a subgenre of science fiction set in a dystopian future, characterised by a focus on "lowlife and high tech". William Gibson's 1984 novel Neuromancer helped solidify the genre, and the 1982 film Blade Runner is among its early films.
rules: Night, rain and haze, in purple with amber windows and neon accents
Neon signs on towers: bars, arrows and rings in magenta, amber and violet, with glow
A wet road that reflects the lights, softened by a blur
Rain streaks and ripples on the ground
Signs that flicker now and then, keyed to the frame number
forms.timing: Drawn on twos, 12 changes a second: rain falls, signs flicker and ripples spread.
build: Draw the city to an off-screen canvas, then draw it again flipped below the horizon with `globalAlpha` 0.4 and `blur()` for the reflection
Signs: a stroked shape with `shadowBlur`, hidden on a few frames from a modulo of `frameOf(t, 12)`
Rain: slanted short lines with seeded positions and speeds; ripples: ellipses that grow and fade
Add a haze gradient near the horizon and a vignette
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: A low synth drone, rain, distant traffic and a hum from the signs. Practice note.
pitfalls: Daylight or flat lighting
A dry road with no reflection
Teal and orange only: this skill leaves teal out; keep to purple, amber and magenta
forms.thin: Wikipedia describes the genre in fiction; the look rules (rain, wet reflections, signs) are a practice summary of how it is usually pictured.

forms.name: ASCII art
forms.what: A scene drawn only from monospaced text characters chosen by brightness: a sunrise over a sea and a headland, with waves, glitter and birds that move.
forms.origin: ASCII art is a graphic design technique of pictures pieced together from the 95 printable characters of the ASCII standard of 1963. Among the oldest examples are works by Kenneth Knowlton from around 1966, and it was invented in large part because early printers lacked graphics ability.
rules: Only characters from one monospaced font: no lines, no shapes
Brightness maps to a ramp of characters from sparse to dense: space, dot, colon, plus, hash, at-sign
A tight grid: about 120 columns and 45 rows
One or two colours on a near-black ground, brighter for denser characters
Motion comes from the character values changing, not from moving glyphs
forms.timing: The picture is recomputed 12 times a second; waves and glitter change on each step.
build: Choose a grid (`cols`, `rows`) and compute a brightness function `lum(u, v, t)` for each cell
Map brightness to a ramp: `RAMP[Math.floor(L * (RAMP.length - 0.01))]`
Draw a row as a few strings, one per brightness bucket, with spaces where another bucket has the character, so that monospace alignment holds and a row costs a few `fillText` calls
Scale horizontally so that the columns fill the frame
For a real image, sample a downscaled copy of it instead of the function
forms.assets: All in code. For video, sample frames and map their luminance.
forms.sound: A dial-up modem, key clicks, a slow arpeggio. Practice note.
pitfalls: A proportional font: the grid breaks
Too few columns: the picture does not read
Too much contrast between neighbouring characters

forms.name: 1-bit dither
forms.what: Two colours only, ink and paper: gradients and shaded forms turned into patterns of pure dots, in a window with a striped title bar, like an early desktop computer.
forms.origin: Ordered dithering applies a preset threshold map tiled across an image to display a continuous image with fewer colours; with the common Bayer map it leaves noticeable crosshatch patterns. A common use of dither is converting a grayscale image to black and white so that the density of black dots approximates the grey level.
rules: Exactly two colours: near-black ink and warm paper white
Grey is made only from the density of dots, in a regular crosshatch pattern
Hard, unsmoothed pixels, scaled up by whole numbers
Title bars with ruled stripes and square widgets
No anti-aliasing and no half-tones
forms.timing: Drawn on twos, 12 changes a second.
build: Render a small buffer (480 by 270), compute a grey `L` for each pixel, and set it to ink or paper by `L > bayer(x, y)` (`bayer()` in `looks-screen.js`)
Draw the buffer scaled by 2 with `imageSmoothingEnabled = false`
Draw the window chrome after the dither, in pure ink and paper with square corners
Real route: a `ShaderPass` that thresholds against an 8 by 8 Bayer matrix
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: A beeper, a floppy-drive whirr, simple square-wave notes. Practice note.
pitfalls: Grey or colour anywhere
Error-diffusion noise instead of an ordered pattern
Smooth scaling that blurs the dots

forms.name: CRT terminal
forms.what: An amber phosphor terminal: text typed one character at a time, a block cursor, scanlines, glow, a slow rolling bar, and a screen that bulges at the middle.
forms.origin: A computer terminal is a device for entering data into, and displaying data from, a computer. Teleprinters were used as early hard-copy terminals and predated computer screens by decades; with inexpensive video displays terminals improved. A cathode-ray tube is the vacuum tube with a fluorescent screen that such displays used.
rules: One phosphor colour on near-black: amber or green
Text in a monospaced face with a soft glow
Scanlines: dark lines every few pixels
A screen that bulges, with darker corners and a reflection
A blinking block cursor and typed text; a faint flicker and a rolling bar
forms.timing: Characters type at about 36 a second; the cursor blinks twice a second; the picture flickers each frame at 24 changes a second.
build: Draw the screen to an off-screen canvas: black, glowing text with `shadowBlur`, scanlines, a rolling band
Curvature: copy the canvas to the main canvas in 3 px slices, each slightly narrower toward the top and bottom
Type text by slicing each line to the number of characters typed so far; place the cursor at the end of that slice
Add a vignette, a faint highlight arc and a rounded bezel mask
forms.assets: All in code. Use a monospaced font that the system has.
forms.sound: Key clicks and a low mains hum. Practice note.
pitfalls: Straight, flat screen edges
Clean text with no glow
Colour: one phosphor only
forms.thin: The sources describe terminals and cathode-ray tubes; scanlines, glow and curvature are practice rules for the look.

forms.name: Hologram HUD
forms.what: A cyan and blue wireframe turning in the dark, with readouts, bars, a dial, corner brackets, a scan band and a flicker with an occasional slipped strip.
forms.origin: A head-up display (HUD) is any transparent display that presents data without requiring users to look away from their usual viewpoints; HUDs were first developed for military aviation and are now used in commercial aircraft, cars and other applications.
rules: A wireframe: latitude and longitude lines, a ring and a satellite
Cyan and blue light on a near-black navy ground, with glow
HUD furniture: corner brackets, bars with numbers, a dial with ticks
A scan band sweeping down the frame and fine scanlines
Flicker, and now and then a strip that slips sideways
forms.timing: The wireframe turns slowly; the numbers change about every quarter of a second; the band sweeps in about 4 seconds. Drawn at 24 changes a second.
build: Project points on a sphere with a turn and a tilt, and draw only the visible half
Draw each wireframe twice: a blue copy shifted 3 px, then a cyan copy, each with a glow
Bars and numbers from a hash of `Math.floor(frame / 6)` so that they tick
Slip: copy a thin strip of the canvas back onto itself offset by 8 px on random frames
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: A soft electronic hum, data chirps and a low pulse. Practice note.
pitfalls: Green or mint instead of cyan and blue
A solid, shaded model: it should be lines only
A steady, clean picture with no flicker
forms.thin: The source describes the real head-up display. The holographic wireframe look is a science-fiction convention, described here as practice.

forms.name: Thermal camera
forms.what: A false-colour heat map through black, purple, red, orange, yellow and white: a hot head and hands, a warm mug, a cold window, a crosshair, a temperature readout and a colour scale.
forms.origin: Infrared thermography, also called thermal imaging, is a technique in which a thermal camera detects infrared radiation from the surface of objects. Warm objects stand out against cooler backgrounds, so that variations in temperature can be seen with or without visible light.
rules: One heat value per pixel, shown through a fixed palette: black, purple, red, orange, yellow, white
Warm objects are bright and soft-edged; cold ones are dark
A hot head and hands, a warm torso, cooler limbs
A crosshair with a temperature readout and a colour scale bar
Sensor noise and fine scanlines
forms.timing: The figure sways slightly and pulses; the readout changes a few times a second. Drawn at 12 changes a second.
build: Draw a heat field in greys on a small canvas (240 by 135) with `blur(2px)`; hot shapes have bright greys
Read it back with `getImageData` and map each grey through a 256-colour palette table
Scale the result up with smoothing, then draw the HUD in white
Add a little seeded noise to each pixel
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: A soft beep on each reading and a fan hum. Practice note.
pitfalls: Natural colours: the picture is false colour
Hard-edged shapes: heat is blurred
A palette that is not monotonic in brightness
forms.thin: The source describes the technique; the specific palette is the common black-purple-red-yellow-white ramp, described here as practice.

forms.name: Silent film
forms.what: Black and white at about 18 frames a second: grain, scratches, a wandering gate, flicker, an iris that opens and closes on a street scene, and an intertitle card with a framed title.
forms.origin: A silent film is a film without synchronised recorded sound, whose plot or key lines are conveyed by intertitles when necessary. The silent era ran from the 1890s to the 1920s in most countries, and films were almost always accompanied by live music from a pianist, an organist or an orchestra.
rules: Black and white only, with a soft vignette
A slow frame rate: about 18 changes a second
Gate weave: the frame wanders a few pixels, with now and then a jump
Flicker, grain, vertical scratches and dust specks
An iris in and out, and a framed intertitle card in a serif capital face
forms.timing: The iris opens in 0.6 seconds, the scene plays, the iris closes at about 2.1 seconds, and the intertitle holds. Drawn at 18 changes a second.
build: Quantise time with `frameOf(t, 18)`; translate the whole frame by a seeded jitter
Iris: clip to a circle whose radius grows or shrinks with `easeOut` and `easeInOut`
Film damage keyed to the frame: scratches that last two frames, dust, hairs and flicker (`filmDamage()` in `looks-screen.js`)
Intertitle: black card, a double white border and a serif title
Draw only in greys
forms.assets: All in code. Real footage can be graded with a black-and-white filter and given the same damage.
forms.sound: A piano or a small orchestra improvising, a projector whirr. Practice note.
pitfalls: Smooth 24 frames-a-second motion
A clean, steady picture
Sound effects: the era was accompanied by music
forms.route: HyperFrames (canvas), or ffmpeg filters on real footage

forms.name: Newsreel
forms.what: Sepia footage of the 1940s: a train racing past telegraph poles, a slanted headline banner, and a damaged print with scratches, hairs, dust, a burn flash and a jolt of the frame.
forms.origin: A newsreel is a short documentary film of news stories and items of topical interest, prevalent from the 1910s to the late 1960s and typically shown in cinemas before a feature; by the end of the 1960s television news had supplanted the format.
rules: Sepia: a warm brown to cream palette, with no true black or white
A slanted, bold headline banner in a heavy condensed face
A moving subject with strong motion: a train, a parade, a ship
Film damage: scratches, hairs, dust, burns and frame jumps
A vignette and heavy grain
forms.timing: Drawn at 18 changes a second; the train, poles and smoke move at constant speeds, and the damage re-rolls every frame.
build: Build the palette with one function that maps 0..1 to a mix of dark brown and cream (`sepia()` in `looks-screen.js`)
Parallax: poles and ties move at different speeds
Banner: rotate the context by about -0.07 radians and draw a dark bar with cream text
Burn flash: a radial gradient on a random frame; jolt: a few pixels of vertical shift on a few frames
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: A brass fanfare, a narrator's urgent cadence and a projector clatter. Practice note.
pitfalls: Grey instead of sepia
A steady, clean picture
Presenting invented footage as a real archive: this is a style, not a document
forms.route: HyperFrames (canvas), or ffmpeg filters on real footage

forms.name: Film noir
forms.what: High-contrast black and white: a wall striped by light through venetian blinds, a man in a fedora and trench coat under a street lamp, rain slanting through the lamp's cone, and a wet pavement.
forms.origin: Film noir is a Hollywood crime drama that emphasises cynical attitudes and motivations; the classic period is the 1940s and 1950s, with a low-key black-and-white visual style whose roots lie in German expressionist cinematography. The French critic Nino Frank first applied the term to Hollywood films in 1946.
rules: Black and white with deep blacks and bright highlights
Low-key light: most of the frame in shadow
Venetian-blind stripes of light across walls and people
A figure in a hat and long coat, lit from the side
Rain, mist and smoke, lit where a lamp shines
forms.timing: The blind stripes drift slowly, the rain falls, smoke curls and ripples spread; smooth, full frame rate.
build: Stripes: parallelograms drawn with `lighter` at low opacity, drifting with time
A lamp cone: a triangle with a vertical gradient; rain lines brighter inside it
Silhouette the figure first, then add rim lines on the lit edge
Add a vignette and fine grain
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: A muted trumpet, a slow saxophone, rain and distant footsteps. Practice note.
pitfalls: Mid-grey lighting: noir needs black
Colour
Stripes with no direction or drift
forms.route: HyperFrames (canvas), or Blender for a lit 3D scene

forms.name: Archive documentary: pan and zoom over stills
forms.what: A slow pan and zoom over still photographs laid on a desk, each with a white border and a shadow, with a lower-third caption and date that slide in for each picture, over film grain.
forms.origin: The Ken Burns effect is a panning and zooming technique used in film and video from still images, named for the American documentarian Ken Burns. It is principally used when film or video material is not available, giving action to stills by slowly zooming in on subjects of interest and panning from one to another.
rules: A slow, eased camera: zoom in on one photograph, then pan to the next
Photographs with white borders, slight tilts and drop shadows
A lower-third caption and date that slide in for each picture
Film grain, a vignette and a dark desk
Aged photographs: sepia tones and a darkened edge
forms.timing: The camera moves between keyframes with `easeInOut`; a picture is held for 3 to 4 seconds. Smooth, full frame rate.
build: Keyframe the camera as (time, centre x, centre y, zoom) and interpolate with `easeInOut`
Draw the world with `translate(W / 2, H / 2)`, `scale(zoom)`, `translate(-cx, -cy)`
Each photograph: a rotated white frame with `shadowBlur`, a clipped picture, and a radial darkening
Captions slide in from the left with `easeOut` when the camera reaches a new photograph
Real route: animate the position and scale of image layers in HyperFrames
forms.assets: Use only photographs the user owns or may reuse; the pictures here are drawn shapes.
forms.sound: A piano, a cello, an archive-style narrator and room tone. Practice note.
pitfalls: A fast or jerky camera
No border, shadow or desk: the stills must look like objects
Presenting invented pictures as real archive

forms.name: Maths diagram
forms.what: A chalk-on-navy maths explainer: an equation builds term by term, each term in its own colour with its own curve on the plot, then the sum curve draws on and a tangent line slides along it with its slope read out.
forms.origin: A tangent line to a curve at a point is the straight line that just touches the curve there; for a curve y = f(x) it passes through (c, f(c)) with slope f'(c), where f' is the derivative. Chalk on a dark board is the classic surface for showing such working.
rules: One colour per term, used in the equation and again for that term's curve
Axes and a faint grid, a bright sum curve, a gold tangent with a dot at the point of tangency
Terms appear one at a time, in the order the plot is built
Few words: the equation, a derivative line and a slope readout
A navy board with a light chalk dust
forms.timing: Terms appear at 0.3, 1.2 and 2.1 seconds, the sum curve draws from 2.8 to 4 seconds, and the tangent then slides back and forth. Smooth, full frame rate.
build: Map maths coordinates to the screen with two small functions (`X(x)`, `Y(y)`) and draw each curve as a polyline up to a fraction `k` of its length
Measure each piece of the equation with `measureText` so that the next piece starts where the last ended
Tangent: `y0 + m (x - x0)` drawn over `x0 +- 2.2`, with `m = f'(x0)` read out in text
Real route for real maths: Manim (a Python library for mathematical animation) renders the same scene with exact `Axes`, `Tex` and `ValueTracker` objects, then HyperFrames or ffmpeg joins the clip
Add a speckle of white dust over the board colour
forms.assets: All in code here. For typeset equations in a real film, use Manim's LaTeX support.
forms.sound: Chalk taps as each term lands, a calm piano and a clear voice. Practice note.
pitfalls: Every term in the same colour
A wall of text or a crowded plot
A curve that appears all at once, with no build
forms.route: HyperFrames (canvas), or Manim for real maths

forms.name: Sticker explainer
forms.what: Die-cut stickers with a thick white border and a drop shadow pop onto a desk with a bounce: icons and bold word stickers, each tilted a little and swaying.
forms.origin: A sticker is a label of plastic, vinyl or another material with a pressure-sensitive adhesive on one side, used for decoration or for function, in many shapes, sizes and colours.
rules: A thick white border follows each shape, with rounded corners: the die-cut line
A soft drop shadow lifts each sticker off the surface
Bold, saturated flat colour with a thin darker edge
Big, heavy word stickers: one word each
Each tilted a few degrees, and none perfectly aligned
forms.timing: Each sticker pops in over about half a second with an overshoot, one every 0.3 seconds, then sways slightly. Smooth, full frame rate.
build: Describe each silhouette as a `Path2D`; draw it first with a 22 px white stroke and a white fill, with `shadowBlur` for the shadow, then fill the colour on top
Pop-in: scale by `overshoot(prog(t, start, 0.55))`, with a small rise from below
Sway: rotate by a sine of time scaled by how long the sticker has been there
Word stickers: a rounded rectangle with `900` weight text centred in it
forms.assets: All in code. Real icon sets should be ones the user owns or may reuse.
forms.sound: A peel-and-stick pop and a cheerful bouncy bed. Practice note.
pitfalls: A white border of uneven width
No shadow: the stickers look printed on the page
Pop-ins with no overshoot
Too many stickers at once
forms.thin: The source describes stickers as objects; the die-cut explainer look is a practice summary.

forms.name: Memphis design
forms.what: Scattered, playful confetti in the manner of 1980s Memphis design: squiggles and zigzags, triangles, circles and half-circles in red, yellow, blue and pink, black-and-white checks, stripes and dots.
forms.origin: The Memphis Group, also called Memphis Milano, was an Italian design and architecture group founded by Ettore Sottsass and active from 1980 to 1987. Its postmodern work often used plastic laminate and terrazzo and was characterised by colourful, abstract decoration and asymmetrical shapes; the look became a ubiquitous aesthetic of the mid-1980s to mid-1990s.
rules: Bold primary colours with pink and black: red, yellow, blue and pink
Confetti shapes: triangles, circles, half-circles, squiggles and zigzags
Black-and-white patterns: checks, stripes and dots inside shapes
Thick black outlines and asymmetrical, overlapping placement
A pale peach or pink ground, with tiny terrazzo flecks
forms.timing: Shapes pop in over the first 1.6 seconds, then drift and turn slowly. Drawn at 12 changes a second.
build: Place each shape from a hash of its index: type, size, position, colour and spin
Patterns: a 4 by 4 checkerboard, a circle clipped to black stripes, a grid of dots
Squiggle: a sine polyline with a thick round-capped stroke
Pop-in with `overshoot(prog(...))`; drift with a sine of stepped time
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: A bouncy synth-pop bed with clicks and pops. Practice note.
pitfalls: Gradients and soft shadows
Neat alignment: Memphis is deliberately off-kilter
Muted colours
Copying a specific designer's piece

forms.name: Particles
forms.what: Thousands of small glowing particles drift in from all over the frame and settle into a word, hold it, then burst apart and reform.
forms.origin: A particle system is a technique in game physics, motion graphics and computer graphics that uses many minute sprites, 3D models or other graphic objects to simulate "fuzzy" phenomena that are hard to reproduce with conventional rendering; it was introduced in the 1982 film Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan for the Genesis effect.
rules: Thousands of tiny points, each simple
The shape appears only from the points' positions
Glow: bright, additive points on a near-black ground
Colour from position: a gradient across the shape
Staggered motion: each particle starts and arrives at its own time
forms.timing: Gathering takes 2.2 seconds, the word holds with a gentle shimmer, then bursts apart over 1.6 seconds; the cycle is 6.2 seconds. Smooth, full frame rate.
build: Sample a target shape once: draw the word on a hidden canvas and keep the lit pixels every 4 px (`wordPoints()` in `looks-abstract.js`)
Give each particle a seeded start and a target; interpolate with a per-particle delay and `easeOut`
Burst: push each outward at a seeded angle with a slight curl
Draw as small squares with `lighter` compositing
Real route: Three.js `Points` with a position buffer you tween on the GPU, or a particle layer in HyperFrames
forms.assets: All in code. Use your own icon or word: no existing logo.
forms.sound: A rising shimmer for the gather and a soft boom for the burst. Practice note.
pitfalls: Too few particles: the shape does not read
All particles moving in lockstep
Using a real company's logo

forms.name: Liquid metaball (blobs that merge)
forms.what: Glossy liquid blobs that drift, merge and split: a smooth colour gradient from warm to violet, a bright rim, and a soft highlight on each blob.
forms.origin: Metaballs, also known as blobby objects, are organic-looking n-dimensional isosurfaces characterised by their ability to meld together when in close proximity to create single, contiguous objects.
rules: Round blobs that join with smooth necks and part again
A glossy surface: a bright highlight, a rim of light, and a darker side
A smooth colour gradient across the blobs, warm to violet
A dark, simple ground
Slow, floating motion on overlapping paths
forms.timing: Seven blobs drift on sine paths; merges and splits happen as they pass. Smooth, full frame rate.
build: Sum a field `F = sum(r^2 / d^2)` over a low-resolution grid (240 by 135) and treat `F > 1` as inside
